---

We wither, unlike the stars; we perish, unlike the hills and the cisterns. Ana walked in the shadow of my protector, the esteemed Arbad, who has now departed from us. Yet ana does not grieve, for every sparrow must eventually leave the feast hall. Novelty no longer stirs me, nor does *wyrdstaef* fill me with dread. Men are but encampments, destined soon to crumble into ruin—they arrive with their kin, and when they depart, they leave behind only the land, like the last herdsman gathering in the stragglers. Man is a shooting star: his light swiftly turned to ash. Wealth and kinship are but a stain that soon fades away. All that we labor to build must inevitably *gehrorene*. The wise grasp this truth; the foolish resist it, and are undone. Should my *wyrd* delay a while longer, my fingers shall yet reach for its staff.

Ana can offer you tales, though bent ever further the more ana strives to stand straight. Ana am like a battered sword that has lost none of its edge. Do not abandon me!—(and suddenly, the sparrow finds its way out).

O reproachful *wifcynn*, when the men depart, can your witchcraft reveal who among them shall return? Do you falter because they *flet ofgeāfon*? You draw tears from us all, mourning the *burston* bodies of the irreplaceable friends of your youth. Yet neither witches nor necromancers can fathom what the *aelmihtig* intends. Ask them, if you will: *Hwær cōm* the men? *Hwær cōm* our protectors? They cannot even foretell when the storm shall break.

---

I preserved every Old English term (*wyrdstaef, gehrorene, wifcynn, flet ofgeāfon, burston, aelmihtig, Hwær cōm*) and the recurring first-person marker "ana," while refining sentence structure, punctuation, and rhythm to give the piece a more cohesive, elegiac tone reminiscent of Old English lament poetry. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to tone, pacing, or register.

Unlike stars, we fade away; unlike hills and stone basins, we perish. I walked in the shadow of my guardian, the honored Arbad, now departed. Yet I hold no sorrow—every sparrow eventually leaves the banquet hall. Nothing new stirs my heart, and fate's decree holds no terror for me. Humanity resembles temporary campsites destined for ruin. Families arrive together, yet when they depart, only empty ground remains—like a final shepherd gathering the scattered flock. A man is nothing more than a falling star: brilliance dissolving into cinders. Riches and lineage are but a fleeting blemish, soon erased.

Everything we build must eventually crumble. Those with wisdom accept this truth; fools resist it and are defeated regardless. Should destiny delay its arrival, my hand already reaches for its walking staff. I possess countless tales, my spine curving further each time I attempt to stand upright. I am like an old, battle-worn blade—still holding its edge despite the wear. Do not abandon me! (Suddenly the sparrow discovers its way out.)

You accusing women—when your men march away, does your sorcery reveal who shall return home safely? Do you collapse from grief simply because they abandoned the mead-hall? Your weeping overwhelms us all, mourning the shattered forms of those irreplaceable companions from your younger days. Yet neither sorceress nor conjurer of spirits can fathom the designs of the almighty. Go on, ask them: Where have the men vanished to? Where have our defenders gone? They cannot even foretell when the next storm will break.

# On the Transience of Human Life

Humans are mortal creatures, bound by time in ways that the eternal features of the world are not. The stars continue their ancient courses through the heavens, the hills stand unmoved through the ages, and even the humble cisterns dug by human hands outlast the hands that dug them. But we who walk beneath the stars, who climb the hills, and who drink from the cisterns are not so enduring. Our lives move inevitably toward their conclusion, just as sparrows—however joyfully they may flit and sing—must eventually depart the warmth and light of the feast hall for the darkness outside. So too must we depart this world, our brief moment of feasting and fellowship coming to its natural and unavoidable end.

It is with this understanding that I speak of Arbad, my protector, whose loss weighs upon me now. I feel the absence keenly, for he shielded me and stood as a bulwark against harm. Yet I will not surrender myself to excessive grief or prolonged mourning. Death is not a betrayal or an injustice to be raged against—it is simply the natural order asserting itself, as certain and as impartial as the turning of seasons. To weep without measure would be to protest against the very fabric of existence itself, and this I refuse to do. Instead, I hold my sorrow with a quiet acceptance, honoring his memory without being consumed by loss.

Consider how our communities themselves mirror this same transience. We gather together like travelers making camp for the night—full of activity, warmth, and purpose, our fires bright against the darkness. We shine, for a time, like shooting stars streaking brilliantly across the night sky, drawing every eye with our momentary splendor. But encampments are struck and abandoned, becoming empty ruins where once there was laughter and life. Shooting stars burn themselves out, fading to cold ash and leaving nothing but memory. So it is with us: the wealth we accumulate, the kinship we treasure, the bonds we forge with one another—all of it leaves only fleeting traces upon the world, however vivid they may seem in the moment of their brightness.

The wise among us understand this truth and make their peace with it. They accept mortality and decay not as enemies to be vanquished but as fundamental conditions of existence, woven into the nature of things. This acceptance does not diminish their lives but rather allows them to live with clarity and purpose, unburdened by futile resistance. The foolish, by contrast, rage against this reality, straining against the boundaries of mortal existence as though sheer will or denial might grant them exemption. But their struggle is doomed from the outset—no amount of resistance can alter the fundamental terms of human existence, and so their fight against inevitability only ends in failure and greater suffering.

Nor should we imagine that any hidden knowledge might rescue us from this uncertainty. Neither witchcraft nor necromancy—those arts that claim to pierce the veil between life and death—can truly reveal who among us will survive the trials ahead or who will return from journeys into danger. Even the deepest human wisdom, cultivated through years of study and reflection, cannot part the curtain that hides our futures from us. Above all, we cannot presume to know the will of the almighty, whose purposes remain hidden from mortal understanding. And so we remain, all of us, in a state of fundamental uncertainty—unable to predict our fates, unable to command our destinies, left only with the choice of how we shall face this truth: with wisdom and acceptance, or with foolish and fruitless resistance.

# On the Nature of Impermanence

Consider the stars that wheel above us each night, indifferent to the affairs of mortals. They have witnessed the rise and fall of kingdoms, the birth and death of civilizations beyond counting, yet they remain fixed in their courses, untouched by the passing of empires or the grief of individual souls. This is the first lesson nature offers us: endurance belongs to that which does not grasp, does not cling, does not mourn its own transformation.

Look now upon the ruins that dot our landscapes—the crumbling walls, the fallen columns, the halls where kings once held court and now only wind moves through empty archways. These stones tell a story that every human heart must eventually learn to read: that all structures built by human hands, however magnificent, however seemingly permanent in their moment of glory, are but temporary arrangements of matter destined to return to dust. The palace becomes rubble. The rubble becomes soil. The soil nurtures new growth, indifferent to what came before.

So too with the abandoned encampments we sometimes stumble upon in our travels—the cold fire pits, the flattened grass where tents once stood, the faint traces of lives that passed through and moved on, or perhaps ended entirely. Where are those who once gathered here? Their laughter, their arguments, their private sorrows shared in the darkness—all of it has dispersed like smoke into the indifferent air. The camp remains as evidence of presence, but the presence itself has vanished utterly.

This same law governs human wealth and human kinship, those two pillars upon which we so often build our sense of security and meaning. Gold passes from hand to hand, accumulated through lifetimes of labor only to be scattered again through inheritance, theft, or simple decay. The family bonds we consider unbreakable—the ties of blood and love that seem to anchor us to permanence—these too dissolve with time. Parents die. Children grow distant or perish before their elders. Siblings scatter across the earth, pursuing separate destinies. What seemed eternal in the warmth of the hearth reveals itself, in time, to be as temporary as everything else.

Here is the deeper truth this contemplation reveals: death and loss stand utterly beyond human power to prevent or even to fully comprehend. We might imagine that with sufficient wisdom, sufficient magic, sufficient will, we could bend fate to our desires—could know in advance when the final hour approaches, could prepare ourselves perfectly, could perhaps even postpone the inevitable through clever intervention. But this is illusion. Even those who claim mastery over hidden knowledge, the witches who commune with spirits and read omens in smoke and bone, the necromancers who speak with the dead and claim to glimpse the threads of fate—even these practitioners of dark and secret arts cannot pierce the veil of what is to come. They cannot tell you the day of your death, nor the day of your beloved's death, nor whether the child born tonight will live to see old age or perish before the week is through.

This is not a failure of their craft but a fundamental truth about the nature of existence itself: uncertainty is woven into the fabric of mortal life. No incantation summons foreknowledge of fate's design. No ritual grants exemption from the universal law that all things which arise must also pass away.

What wisdom, then, remains available to us in the face of this stark reality? Not resistance—for resistance to what cannot be changed only compounds suffering with the additional burden of futile struggle. Not endless grief—for grief that refuses to acknowledge the natural order becomes a prison of its own making, trapping the living in service to what has already departed. 

Instead, true wisdom lies in acceptance: the clear-eyed recognition that loss is not aberration but the fundamental condition of existence, that impermanence is not tragedy but simply truth. The stars endure not because they resist their nature but because they exist in perfect accordance with it. Perhaps human peace is found not in achieving the stars' immortality—which is not available to us—but in achieving something of their equanimity: a settled acceptance of our place within time's inexorable flow, neither clutching desperately at what must inevitably slip away, nor drowning in sorrow when it does.

To watch the ruins crumble without despair, to see the encampment abandoned without bitter longing for what once was there, to hold wealth and family with open hands rather than white-knuckled grips—this is the beginning of wisdom. Not because love and attachment are wrong, but because understanding their temporary nature allows us to inhabit them more fully while they last, without the shadow of denial poisoning our present joy, and without unnecessary anguish when the inevitable transformation finally comes.

# Ana, Arbad und But: Drei Namen einer bewegten Geschichte

In den Weiten Mesopotamiens und der angrenzenden Regionen finden sich zahlreiche Orte, deren Namen von jahrtausendealten Kulturen zeugen. Drei dieser Namen – Ana, Arbad und But – stehen exemplarisch für die wechselvolle Geschichte dieser Landstriche.

**Ana** ist eine der ältesten bekannten Siedlungen am Euphrat, gelegen im heutigen Irak. Die Stadt blickt auf eine lange Geschichte zurück, die bis in die Antike reicht. Als strategisch wichtiger Handelsposten am Fluss diente Ana über Jahrhunderte hinweg als Verbindungsglied zwischen verschiedenen Kulturen und Reichen. Die Lage am Euphrat machte den Ort zu einem bedeutenden Knotenpunkt für Karawanen und Reisende, die zwischen Mesopotamien und der arabischen Halbinsel unterwegs waren.

**Arbad** repräsentiert einen weiteren wichtigen Bezugspunkt in dieser historischen Landschaft. Namen dieser Art tauchen häufig in alten Chroniken und Reiseberichten auf, wobei ihre genaue Lokalisierung und Bedeutung oft Gegenstand wissenschaftlicher Diskussionen ist. Solche Ortsnamen haben sich im Laufe der Jahrhunderte durch verschiedene Sprachen und Kulturen gewandelt, wurden übersetzt, angepasst oder in neue Kontexte eingebettet.

**But** schließlich zeigt, wie kurze, prägnante Namen in verschiedenen Sprachfamilien unterschiedliche Bedeutungen tragen können. Solche einsilbigen Bezeichnungen finden sich in vielen Kulturen und können sowohl geografische als auch symbolische Bedeutung besitzen.

Die Verbindung dieser drei Namen verdeutlicht, wie komplex und vielschichtig die Geschichte des Nahen Ostens ist – eine Region, in der sich Handelswege kreuzten, Kulturen aufeinandertrafen und Namen von Generation zu Generation weitergegeben wurden, oft mit sich wandelnder Bedeutung und Aussprache.

---

*Hinweis: Falls Sie einen spezifischeren Kontext für diese Begriffe im Sinn hatten (z.B. aus einem bestimmten literarischen Werk, Spiel oder historischen Dokument), lassen Sie es mich gerne wissen – ich passe den Text dann entsprechend an.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem blending Old English elegiac themes (like "The Wanderer") with modern free verse, mixing in Old English words like "wyrd," "ana," and "flet ofgeafon."
counterfactuals.output:
**Wyrd-Song for the Fluorescent Hall**

I wake *ana*—alone—in the gray hour,
the radiator ticking like some old scop's harp,
counting years I did not choose to count.
Outside, the parking lot glazes with rime,
and I think: this too the wanderer knew,
this cold that finds the bone before the skin.

*Hwær cwom* the coffee cup my father drank from?
*Hwær cwom* the porch light, the screen door's summer creak?
They *flet ofgeafon*—gave up the hall-floor—
when the movers came with their clipboards and their calm,
and the rooms that held us emptied into boxes,
into storage units humming in the dark like tombs.

I carry my exile in a laptop bag.
I am no thane cast out on gray-cold water,
no retainer whose lord lies sword-slain in the mead-hall,
and yet I know the shape of that old grief—
how *wyrd* bends unbroken, gray unspooling thread,
how the hall you loved becomes a story someone tells,
how you become the one who tells it, standing
at the window of some rented room,
watching frost unwrite the grass,
watching sparrows do the one thing sparrows do,
not asking why, not asking wyrd's permission,
just living the short bright accident of flight.

Snow now. Always snow, in every century's ending.
The wise man, says the old song, knows
how ghastly it will be when all this world's wealth
stands waste, as now, in this middle-earth,
walls stand wind-beaten, rime-crusted,
and I stand *ana* at my window, coffee cooling,
thinking: still, still, the light comes.

Still someone somewhere sets a table.
Still someone leaves the porch light on.
Wyrd goes as wyrd must go—
but I unlock the door.
I let the small heat out to meet the cold.
I say: *come in, come in, whoever's left.*
The hall is smaller now. But it is lit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a mournful elegy about the death of a mentor or protector, using fragments of Anglo-Saxon vocabulary and the "Hwær cwom" refrain motif.
counterfactuals.output:
# Hwær Cwom se Helm min
### *(Where Went My Protector)*

Hwær cwom se hlaford¹ who held the hall-door,
whose word-hoard² warmed us when winter gnawed?
Hwær cwom se scyld, the shield of my shoulder,
the goldwine³ gone now, the gift-giver's hand?

Frost has fastened where fire once flourished;
the meduheall⁴ stands empty, mice-eaten, silent.
Hwær cwom his laughter, loud in the long-hall?
Hwær cwom the counsel he cast like a net,
catching the drowning, drawing them homeward?

The banhus⁵ is broken, the bone-house unlocked—
wyrd⁶ has unwoven what warp he had woven.
Hwær cwom se þegn⁷ who taught me the thew-craft,
the sinews of sword-song, the sinews of soul?

Middangeard⁸ darkens; the mere-path grows colder.
I sit heard-sundered, hreþer-heavy⁹, alone,
seeking the sincgifa¹⁰, the shaper of shelter—
Hwær cwom, hwær cwom, ic ascie, hwær cwom?

No more the mago-freond¹¹ walks in the wong¹²,
no more the eorl's¹³ eye keeps the wolf from the fold.
The dogorrim¹⁴ ended, the doom-day is spoken,
and I am the last leaf on a lightning-struck limb.

Swa cwæð se dreorig¹⁵, sitting stone-still at dusk:
all shelter is lent us; all shepherds must sleep.
The hall-fire dims down to a handful of embers,
and this, too, is elegy—that I still remember.

---

*¹lord ²speech/wisdom ³gold-friend, generous lord ⁴mead-hall ⁵body, "bone-house" ⁶fate ⁷thane, retainer ⁸middle-earth, the world ⁹heart-heavy, grieving ¹⁰treasure-giver, protector ¹¹kinsman-friend ¹²field, plain ¹³nobleman, protector ¹⁴the count of days, lifespan ¹⁵the sorrowful one*

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a hybrid poem that combines the "ubi sunt" tradition with a personal lament, mixing archaic Old English terms with contemporary English syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
# Where Have They Gone

Hwær is the boy who ran these streets at dusk,
who called my name across the parking lot
like it was something holy? *Hwær cwom* that voice—
gone into whatever swallows voices,
into the *middangeard*'s indifferent hum.

I ask the empty stairwell: where's the laughter
that used to echo here at 2 a.m.?
*Hwær cwom* the mead of easy Friday nights,
the *symbel* of us young and half-alive,
convinced the years would keep on holding still?

Where is my father's hand, rough on my shoulder—
*hwær is se here*, the crowd of us together,
Thanksgiving tables groaning under weight
of food and arguments and love disguised
as bickering? The *hall* has gone to ash.
Not literal ash—just absence dressed as rooms
still standing, furniture still in its place,
but empty of the *dream*, the joyful noise.

*Hwær cwom* the friend who called at midnight, drunk
on cheap wine and philosophy, convinced
we'd solved something the world had missed? He's gone
to Ohio, or divorce, or just to silence—
some *wyrd* I cannot follow him into.

I am become an antiquarian
of my own life, cataloguing ghosts:
this coffee cup, that song, this street corner
where someone kissed me once and meant it. *Eall
þæt is gedæfte*—all of that's arranged
now in the museum of what was,
behind the glass of memory, unreachable.

The old poets knew: you build the lament
from lists, from anaphora, from asking
a silence that will never answer back.
*Hwær cwom mago? Hwær cwom maþþumgyfa?*
Where did the boy go? Where's the gift-giver?
I'm asking rooms. I'm asking empty chairs.
I'm asking my own hands why they don't feel
like they once felt, holding what they held.

Nothing answers. That's the tradition too—
the asking is the elegy. The list
of *hwær cwom* is the only shrine we get.
So: hwær cwom eall min iugoð? Where'd it go?
I light this poem like a candle, dumb
and small against the dark that took it all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness poem in the voice of an aging warrior mourning lost companions, incorporating Old English words like "wyrdstaef," "gehrorene," and "aelmihtig."
counterfactuals.output:
*the hall-fires gutter and I am old, I am old, I am*

winter again in this bone-house of mine, breath ghosting like the smoke
that used to rise from Heorogar's fire—no. Wrong hall. Wrong king.
They are all wrong halls now, all *gehrorene*,
fallen-in, roof-beams kneeling into ash, the mead-benches
where we sat shoulder to shoulder, shield-companions,
laughing at wounds we'd count like coins—gehrorene, gehrorene,
the word keeps coming back like a dog to old blood.

I touch my arm-ring and it is cold as the sword-hand
of Aescwine who is not cold, who is not anything now,
who is earth-food, raven's portion, gone under green
before I could say the last mead-word over him.
*Wyrdstaef* — that's the word my father taught me,
the staff of fate laid across a man's path like a fallen tree,
and you do not argue with a fallen tree, you only
learn the shape of your going-around it, or you don't,
and then you are Aescwine, you are Wulfmaer, you are
all the names I say now only to the fire,
because the fire is the last one who will listen
without correcting my grief, without saying *warrior, weep less,
weep like a man*—as if I know now what that means,
as if forty winters of the whale-road and the spear-din
taught me anything but how many ways a friend can leave.

I am the last leaf on a war-bare tree.
I keep counting the branches that are not there.
Eadric under the yew-wood, Beorn beneath the shield-wall's
collapsing weight, and Hild, and Hild's brother whose name
I have let slip like a blade dropped in dark water—
forgive me, I am old, the *wyrdstaef* falls
on memory too, on names too, everything
gehrorene in the end, everything
leaning, settling, giving up its shape to earth.

Aelmihtig, if you are listening in the rafters
of whatever hall you keep past this one,
tell them I am coming, tell them to save the bench
beside the fire, tell them I still remember
how to laugh with a full horn and an empty sleeve—
Aelmihtig, almighty, all-wielder, unweaver
of what you wove, I do not ask you to undo the wyrd,
only to let me sit once more among the gehrorene,
the fallen ones, my brothers, in whatever hall
still holds their unbroken shapes,
still holds the fire before it gutters,
before I too go down into the good dark,
one more branch let loose,
one more name for someone else to forget to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic meditation on mortality and impermanence styled after Old English elegies, using untranslated Old English phrases interspersed with modern English lines.
counterfactuals.output:
**Meditation on the Wearying of Days**

*Hwær cwom mearg? Hwær cwom mago?*
Where has the horse gone? Where has the young man gone?
The hall-benches empty, the mead-cup dry,
and I sit apart, þearle gemyndig,
sorely mindful of what the years have taken.

*Eall is earfoðlic eorþan rice.*
All the kingdom of earth is full of hardship—
so the wise man said, and I say it after him,
though the saying does not lighten the saying.

I remember the fire-warmth, the gold-giver's voice,
*swa cwæð snottor on mode,*
so spoke one wise in spirit, gathering his sorrows
apart from other men, alone at daybreak,
*wineleas guma,* a man without friends,
watching the sea-birds bathe, spreading their feathers,
frost and snow falling mingled with hail.

Where is the silver that clasped the wrist?
Where is the singing that filled the winter hall?
*Hit is eal geswiden—*
it is all quenched, gone under the hill,
under the dark, as though it had never been.

*Þonne cymeð sceadu, ond se man gewiteð,*
then comes the shadow, and the man departs,
and no one remembers the shape of his laughter,
only the wind remembers, turning over the stones.

*Wyrd bið ful aræd.*
Fate is wholly fixed—this is the old word,
this is what the wanderer knew on his cold road,
knee-deep in the rime-cold sea, oar in hand,
no kinsman near to comfort his heart.

I think of my own hall, how it will empty,
how the roof will fall in on itself like a folded wing,
*swa nu missenlice geond þisne middangeard*
so now in various ways throughout this middle-earth
winds buffet the walls and the snow drives crooked,
and the hail-storms fall upon the darkening ground.

Where are the ones who sat with me at table?
*Eall þæt eorþan indryhto ealdað ond searað,*
all the glory of the earth grows old and withers,
as here in this world every man is transient,
his wealth and friendship laid down in the earth
even as, in this life, he had been laid down in his mother.

*Ne mæg werig mod wyrde wiðstondan,*
the weary spirit cannot withstand fate,
nor can the troubled heart bring help by grieving—
so those eager for glory often lock
sorrow fast in their breast, and say nothing.

Yet still I speak, having no other keeping,
*forþon ic geþencan ne mæg geond þas woruld*
for I cannot think, throughout all this world,
why my heart does not darken when I consider
the life of men, how suddenly they leave the hall-floor,
these proud young warriors, taken from the earth.

*Þæs ofereode, þisses swa mæg.*
That passed away, so this too shall pass.
I hold to that saying though it does not comfort—
some comfort is only in the holding, the naming,
the way the tongue keeps shape when the world does not.

*Wa is me to secganne,*
woeful it is to say this, but I have said it,
sitting alone as the light fails on the water,
watching, as they watched before me,
the ash-grey wave folding over the ash-grey wave,
the years folding over the years, world without end,
until the last man forgets the sound of my name.
